answer.exemplar: A sample supports a claim about a population only when the sample was drawn in a way that could have represented that population and when it is large enough for the differences it is being asked to reveal. A survey of 40 shoppers taken inside one supermarket fails on the first count, because the customers of a single store are selected by where that store is, what it stocks, and its prices, and none of that resembles the shopper population of a country. The bias does not average out with a larger sample, so repeating the survey there would make it more reliable about that supermarket and no more reliable about the country. The second count is a separate matter: even a random sample of 40 could miss a genuine small difference simply by chance, so a survey that reports 42 of 70 as 60 percent can support a statement about the share in that sample and about the population only with an explicit margin of error attached. What would be needed instead is a sample drawn from across the whole population by a method that gives every member a known chance of selection, together with a statement of how wide the uncertainty is. A count taken at one location can be scaled up to a population only when the proportion it measures is assumed to hold everywhere, and that assumption is precisely what the single-site survey cannot test.

questions.explanation: A strong answer separates the two separate problems with the survey. The first is selection, since shoppers at one store were never given a chance of being picked and are not a cross section of the country, and that bias does not shrink with more shoppers. The second is size, since even a fair sample of 40 carries uncertainty that has to be reported. The remedy in each case is specific: random selection from across the population, and a stated margin of error.
questions.hint: Separate the problem of who was chosen from the problem of how many were chosen.
questions.learningObjective: explain why a sample cannot support a population claim and what would be required

answer.exemplar: A deductive argument is valid when its conclusion cannot fail to be true if its premises are true, and validity is a matter of form alone, so a valid deductive argument with true premises guarantees its conclusion completely. All cats are mammals and this animal is a cat, therefore this animal is a mammal, is deductively valid, and nothing about the world can make it come out false. The guarantee is total but it buys nothing extra, because the conclusion adds no information beyond what the premises already contained, and a single counterexample shows that a valid-looking form is in fact invalid. An inductive argument is different in kind: some cats are black, every cat observed so far has been black, therefore this cat is probably black. Nothing forces the conclusion, since a white cat would leave every premise true and the conclusion false, so the argument is not deductively valid at all. What an induction offers instead is strength in the sense of support, and that support is a matter of how well the premises were chosen, how many observations were made, and how much they resembled the case being predicted. Because that support can be strong without being certain, a good inductive argument is one whose evidence is relevant and plentiful, and a weak one is one that generalises from a single untypical case.

questions.explanation: A complete answer states that a valid deductive argument makes its conclusion unavoidable, so the conclusion cannot be false while the premises are true, whereas an inductive conclusion can be false however true the premises are. The examples should show that clearly, with a cat that is a mammal against a cat that is probably black. Worth adding that a deductive conclusion adds no information beyond its premises, while an inductive conclusion can be well supported without being certain, which is why the two kinds of support are not comparable.
questions.hint: Ask whether there is any way for the premises to be true and the conclusion false.
questions.learningObjective: compare the strength of valid deductive and inductive arguments

answer.exemplar: Every cat is a mammal, and its contrapositive is every animal that is not a mammal is not a cat. The two are equivalent because a conditional and its contrapositive say the same thing with the words and not flipped, so a truth table has identical columns for the two forms, and that is what makes the reversal legitimate. The converse, that every mammal is a cat, is a different statement, and it is false: a dog is a mammal and is not a cat, so the converse has a counterexample. That single dog is enough, because the converse is a universal claim and one failure defeats it, whereas the contrapositive is refuted only by a case that makes the original conditional false, which no cat and no non-mammal can do. The asymmetry is easy to remember by counting: the contrapositive swaps both the hypothesis and the conclusion and negates both, whereas the converse swaps them and negates neither, and swapping alone is not a safe operation. In practice the error is common, because language is full of conditionals whose converse happens to be true often enough to seem reliable, and the sample then hides a false rule.

questions.explanation: The explanation should build both forms from the original and then show why only one of them survives. Negating the condition and the conclusion together reverses a conditional without changing its truth, while swapping them without negating either does not, and a truth table shows the two columns matching for the contrapositive and not for the converse. The counterexample has to be named, and a dog defeats the converse that every mammal is a cat while leaving the original conditional untouched.
questions.hint: Write out all three forms and check each one against a single case that the original allows.
questions.learningObjective: explain the equivalence of a conditional and its contrapositive and refute its converse

answer.exemplar: The model says that each patient's waiting time is drawn independently of every other patient, which in practice means the clinic assumes that whoever happens to be waiting has no effect on how long the next patient will wait. That assumption is invisible in the data until something breaks it, and the way to expose it is to look for waiting times that move together. Record the arrival time and the waiting time of every patient for a week and then plot one against the other, and a model that holds will produce a cloud with no structure, because knowing when a patient arrived would tell you nothing about how long they waited. The failure has a clear signature: if patients arriving in the busy late-morning stretch all wait longer, then a point with a late arrival time and a long wait is evidence that a queue exists, and the same pattern shows up as a time-of-day effect on the mean waiting time, with the busiest period's mean far above the quietest. A second signature appears when an unusually long wait is followed by a run of short ones, since a genuinely independent wait would not leave the next patient's wait short. Neither signature proves the model wrong on its own, because a busy season could do the same thing, but both make the assumption testable, which is what separates an assumption that can be checked from one that simply cannot.

questions.explanation: A good answer turns the assumption into something that can be looked for in data rather than restating it. Independence predicts that the time of arrival carries no information about the length of the wait, so plotting one against the other should show an unstructured cloud, and a visible structure, a busy-period effect on the mean, or a long wait followed by a run of short ones would each count against the model. Saying only that the assumption is uncertain would not answer what to go and measure.
questions.hint: Say what the assumption predicts the data should look like if it were true.
questions.learningObjective: identify the data that would expose a violation of a stated modelling assumption

questions.explanation: A negation denies the whole of the statement it sits in front of, so the negation of p is not p, and it is true exactly when p is false. A double negation denies the denial, which restores the original, so not not p is the same statement as p in every situation. The cancellation only works when the two negations are properly matched, and it is worth writing the truth table to see that not p and p are opposites while not not p and p agree in every row.
questions.hint: Ask whether the statement being affirmed or denied, then count how many denials there are.
questions.learningObjective: form the negation of a statement and simplify a double negation

questions.explanation: A conditional fails in exactly one situation, namely when the condition is true and the conclusion is not, so the single false row is p true with q false and the other three rows are true. That is why a conditional is not the same statement as p and q together, which would be true in only one row, and it is why a conditional whose condition is false is true whatever the conclusion says. Counting the three other rows as false is the reversal of the whole pattern.
questions.hint: Look for the row where the condition holds and the conclusion does not.
